en: Aitareya Upaniṣad: Peace Recitation. Om! May my speech be established in my mind; may my mind be established in my speech. Be manifest and bring me prosperity.
You are the two pins of my Veda; do not let what I have heard fall away from me.
By this study, I join together the days and nights; I shall speak the Ṛta;
I shall speak the Truth.
May that protect me; may it protect the speaker;
may it protect me, may it protect the speaker, may it protect the speaker.
Oṃ peace! Peace! Peace!
The discussion on the relationship [between ritual action and knowledge] is concluded; thus, ritual action, together with the knowledge of the lower Brahman, has reached its ultimate goal.
This supreme attainment of action conjoined with knowledge has been summarized by means of the knowledge of the *uktha*.

"It is this truth, the Brahman called Prāṇa"; "This is the one God"; "All the gods are but manifestations of this very Prāṇa"; "Attaining the state of identity with this Prāṇa, one goes to the gods"—thus it has been said.
This attainment of the gods, characterized as such, is the supreme human goal; this is liberation (mokṣa).
Some maintain that this is to be attained through the means consisting of the combination of knowledge and action as previously described, and that there is nothing higher than this.
Desiring to set those [views] aside, the text beginning with "The Self, verily, this [was]" (*ātmā vā idam*) was spoken for the purpose of enjoining the knowledge of the absolute Self alone.
But how is it understood that the subsequent section is intended for enjoining the knowledge of the absolute Self, which is unrelated to ritual action? Because no other purpose is perceived.

And thus, the text will later demonstrate that the aforementioned deities, such as Agni and others, are subject to transmigratory existence by showing them to possess defects such as hunger and thirst, in the passage beginning with, “Him [Agni] they assailed with hunger and thirst” (1.2.1).

Everything characterized by hunger and the like is indeed within the realm of *saṃsāra*; for the Supreme Brahman, however, there is the scriptural declaration of the transcendence of hunger and so forth.

This being so, knowledge of the Self alone is the means to liberation; yet, in this context, one who is devoid of ritual action (*akarmī*) is not entitled [to this knowledge], because no specific qualification to that effect is heard in the scripture.
Because no other stage of life (āśrama) is mentioned here for one who is not engaged in ritual action;
and because, immediately after introducing the ritual action characterized by the thousand Bṛhatī verses, the knowledge of the Self is commenced.
Therefore, it is only the performer of rituals who is qualified [for this].
Nor is the knowledge of the Self unrelated to karma, because of the concluding summary as before.

Just as for the person connected with karma who has the sun as his self, his being the self of all living beings—both stationary and moving—was stated by the Brāhmaṇa and the mantra beginning with "The sun is the Self" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.114.1), in the very same way [it is said]: "He is Brahman, he is Indra" (3.1.1).
3) Beginning with these words, [the text] will conclude by stating that [Brahman] is the self of all living beings: "And whatever is stationary, all that has wisdom as its guide" (3.1.3).
Likewise, in the *Saṃhitopaniṣad*: "For the Bahvṛcas indeed investigate this very [Self] in the Great Hymn" (Ai.Ā. 3.2.3).
12) Having stated [the soul's] connection with karma through such passages, he concludes: “In all beings, they call this very one ‘Brahman’.
Likewise, for that same [soul] which was described as “this bodiless conscious self,” its oneness is stated: “One should know that this [self] and that which is in the sun are one and the same.
Here too, [the question is asked]: “Who is this self? (3.1.1).
1) Having begun thus, [the text] will demonstrate that the very nature of the Self is wisdom in the passage, “Brahman is consciousness” (3.1.3).
Therefore, the knowledge of the Self is not connected with ritual action.

If it is argued that there is the fault of tautology and meaninglessness— asking how so— if it is claimed that the re-determination of the Self, following the prior determination by the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with “O Ṛṣi, I am indeed Prāṇa” and by the mantra “The Sun is the Self,” constitutes a tautology and is therefore meaningless when presented again by way of a question, we say: no.
There is no fault of redundancy because this [passage] serves to determine specific attributes of that very [Self].

How so? Because it serves to determine specific attributes—such as the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world—belonging to that very agent of action, or because its purpose is solely for the sake of meditation (*upāsti*).

Alternatively, the subsequent textual sequence beginning with "the Self" (*ātman*) has the following meaning: since meditation on the Self as an agent of action might not have been established apart from his ritual duties during the discussion of karma, it is intended to show that the Self is to be meditated upon even independently.

Because he is to be meditated upon both as distinct and non-distinct, the Self is indeed one; in the sphere of ritual action, He partakes of the perception of distinction, yet at the time when there is no action, He is likewise to be meditated upon as non-distinct—thus there is no tautology.
"He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together..."

"Having crossed over death through ignorance, one attains immortality through knowledge" (Isha Upanishad 11), and "Performing actions here alone, one should desire to live a hundred years," as stated in the Vajasaneyi Upanishad (2).
Furthermore, the maximum lifespan of mortals does not exceed a hundred years,
by which [limited] abandonment of action one might worship the Self;
for it has been shown that "the days of a man's lifespan amount to so many thousands."
Furthermore, a lifespan of a hundred years is pervaded by action alone.
And the mantra has been shown: “Only performing actions here,” and so forth;
likewise, “One should offer the Agnihotra as long as one lives,” and “One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa rites as long as one lives,” and so on.

And [it says], "They burn him with the sacrificial vessels. Furthermore, there is the scriptural teaching regarding the three debts; in that context, the scripture concerning renunciation and so forth states: "Having stepped out [from the household], they then lead the life of a mendicant" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1, 4.4.22).
22) Thus, this is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended to praise the knowledge of the Self, or it has a subject matter not [directly] enjoined [as a duty].
This is not so; for when the fruit is not perceived in the realization of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), ritual action (*kriyā*) is untenable.
As for what was said—that the knowledge of the Self belongs to the agent and is connected with ritual action—that is not so.

For when one realizes through direct cognition that "I am Brahman"—the Supreme, whose desires are fulfilled and who is free from all defects of transmigratory existence—one perceives no purpose for the Self in either what has been done or what remains to be done; and in the absence of a perceived result, ritual action is not possible.
If it is argued that one acts because of being enjoined even when no fruit is seen, we say no; for [such a person] perceives the Self as being beyond the scope of injunction.

In the world, it is observed that the object of an injunction is one who perceives the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired as his purpose and thus seeks the means to that end. However, one who perceives the identity of Brahman and the Self—which is the opposite of that—is not an object of injunction.

Even if one were a knower of the identity of Brahman and the Self, if they were still subject to injunction, then since there would be no one who is not a fit object for an injunction, it would follow that every action must be performed by everyone at all times;
and that is undesirable. Furthermore, such a person cannot be enjoined by anyone.
For the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) also originates from that [the Veda];
indeed, one is not enjoined by a word arising from one's own cognition,
nor is a master of great wisdom by a servant lacking discrimination.
If it is argued that because the Veda is eternal, it possesses the capacity to enjoin everyone by virtue of its independence, we say no; for the aforementioned defect remains.
Even so, the defect—that the entire ritual must be performed by everyone at all times without distinction—is indeed unavoidable.

If it is further argued that this too is enjoined by the scripture itself—just as the performance of rituals was established by the scripture, so too is this knowledge of the Self enjoined by the scripture for that very same ritualist—we reply: [this is not so].
No; for it is impossible for [the word] to convey contradictory meanings.

Indeed, it is not possible to convey both the state of being connected with what has been done and its opposite in relation to a single thing, just as one cannot convey both coldness and heat in fire.
The desire to unite with what is desired and the desire to separate from what is undesired are not produced by the treatise (*śāstra*),
because they are observed in all living beings.
If those two were produced by the treatise, they would not be seen in cowherds and the like.
This is because they are ignorant of the scriptures.
For that which is not attained by itself must be made known by the scripture;
and if that knowledge of the Self—which is contrary to the performance of ritual acts—has been established by the scripture, [then...]
How could it produce again a sense of duty that is contrary to that [knowledge], like coldness in fire or darkness in the sun?
If you say, "It does not awaken [the knowledge] at all," we say no, for [the scripture states]: "He should know: 'That is my Self'" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.8).
9) Also because of the concluding statement: “Prajñāna is Brahman” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28),
and “Then he knew only himself” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10).
9) Because statements such as "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.16) have that [knowledge] as their ultimate purport,
and because the knowledge of Brahman as the Self, once arisen, is not sublated, it cannot be said that it has not arisen or that it is erroneous.

If it is argued that the absence of a purpose is equally applicable even in the case of renunciation, [we reply]: no, because of the Smṛti text, "Nothing here is achieved by non-action" (Gītā 3.28). If it is further argued that this same defect—the absence of a purpose—applies equally to those who say that one should renounce the world only after realizing Brahman, we say no;
for renunciation consists merely in the cessation of action.
For the existence of a purpose is caused by ignorance; it is not an inherent property of things, since it is observed in all living beings.
Furthermore, we observe that one who is impelled by thirst for a purpose engages in activity through speech, mind, and body, as in:
"He desired, ‘May I have a wife’" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4).

17) By such statements as these, it is established that the fivefold characteristics (pāṅktalakṣaṇa), such as sons and wealth, are merely objects of desire; for the Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa affirms this with the restrictive statement: "For both of these are indeed desires" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1; 4.4.22).

Since the activity of speech, mind, and body characterized by the fivefold set has ignorance, desire, and defects as its causes, such activity is impossible for the knower because of the absence of defects like ignorance; therefore, renunciation (vyutthāna) is simply the cessation of ritual action.

But it does not have the nature of something to be performed, like a sacrifice or similar act, nor is it of a positive (bhāvātmaka) character; and since it is a quality of the person possessing knowledge, no further purpose need be sought for it.

For when one who has been proceeding in darkness encounters light, the fact that pits, mud, thorns, and so forth are no longer encountered is not a matter for the question, "What is the purpose of this?"

[Objection: "In that case, since one has already attained the goal, there is no need for further instruction regarding renunciation. If the knowledge of the Supreme Brahman has arisen while one is still in the householder's state, let him remain right there without performing [ritual acts]; he need not go elsewhere. [Reply: No, because the householder's state is prompted by desire. As it is said: "Desire is indeed of this extent" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.17), and "For both of these are indeed desires" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1; 4.4.22).
22) Because of this restriction:

the mere absence of a fixed necessity regarding the connection with objects of desire, such as sons, wealth, and so forth, is not what is called "rising" (vyutthāna), which refers to going elsewhere than that.
Therefore, for one in whom knowledge has arisen, there is no remaining in the state of a householder while failing to perform [ritual duties].
By this, it is established that even for the learned man, there is non-performance of service to the teacher and of austerity.

On this point, some householders—fearing the begging rounds and the like, and fearing contempt, while displaying a subtle insight—offer this reply: "Since even for a mendicant rules such as the begging round are observed, [these are necessary] even for a householder who seeks merely the maintenance of the body."

"Let the seat be right in one's own home for one who is free from both the desire for what is to be accomplished and the means of accomplishment, and who subsists on mere food and clothing solely for the purpose of maintaining the body.
No; this has already been answered by the fact that the restriction to the specific possession of one's own home is motivated by desire.

And in the absence of the specific possession of a home, for one who seeks only food and clothing required for the mere maintenance of the body, it follows by implication that they are indeed a mendicant due to the lack of specific possessions. Just as there is a rule for a mendicant regarding the practice of begging for alms and such, as well as regarding purity and so forth,

so too let there be a mandatory engagement in obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) for the wise householder who is free from desire, because he is enjoined by scriptural texts such as "as long as life lasts" (*yāvaj-jīvam*) for the sake of avoiding transgression (*pratyavāya*).
This has already been answered with respect to the knower (*vidvas*), on the grounds that he is not an object of such injunctions and because he cannot be enjoined to what is impossible.

If it is argued that this renders the eternal injunctions, such as "as long as one lives," purposeless, we say no; for they remain meaningful as being intended for those who are not yet knowers (*avidvat*).
As for the necessity of activity in the case of a monk who engages in action solely for the purpose of maintaining the body, that necessity is not the motivator for that activity.
Just as one who performs the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) does so not for the sake of some other purpose— since the cessation of thirst is understood [as the result]—
it is not possible to establish that the Agnihotra and other such rites have a similar necessity of activity that arises from an external purpose.

If it is argued that even the restriction regarding the engagement [in activity] that follows from the attainment of the purpose is untenable in the absence of a motive, we say no; for that restriction is established by prior engagement, and there is a heavy burden of effort involved in its transgression.
Since the renunciation that follows from the attainment of the purpose is stated again, its status as a duty for the wise person is established.
Even for one who is not yet a knower, the life of a wandering mendicant must indeed be undertaken by one desiring liberation;
and to this effect, such scriptural statements as “peaceful and self-controlled” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23) serve as authoritative evidence.
Furthermore, because the means for realizing the Self, such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*), are not possible in other stages of life (*āśrama*s),
it is known from the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*: "He fully proclaimed to those who have transcended the stages of life this supreme purifier, which is cherished by the assembly of sages" (6.21).
And the Kaivalya Śruti says: "Neither by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality" (Kaivalya 2);
and the Smṛti says: "Having known [this], one should practice niṣkarma."

And because it is stated, "One should dwell in the stage of the Brahma-hermitage," and because the means for the knowledge of Brahman, such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and the rest, are found in their entirety among those belonging to no specific order (*atyāśramin*), whereas they are impossible within the householder's life;
furthermore, an incomplete means is not sufficient to accomplish any purpose.

Moreover, regarding those duties of the householder's stage that are useful for the realization of [Brahman], their highest fruit is summarized as merging into the deity, which pertains solely to the realm of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).

If the knowledge of the Supreme Self were intended only for those engaged in ritual action (*karmin*), then the concluding summary of the fruit would have pertained solely to the sphere of transmigratory existence.

If it is argued that this is merely a subordinate fruit (*aṅgaphala*) of the rituals, we say no; for the knowledge of the Self has as its object the reality of the Self which is in contradiction with those [rituals].
Knowledge whose object is the ultimate reality of the Self—the supreme essence in which all names, forms, and actions have been discarded—is the means to immortality.
For if there were a connection between qualities and their results, it would not follow that knowledge has as its object the reality of the Self, which is devoid of all particularities;
and that is undesirable, [as stated in the scripture]: "But where everything has become the Self alone for him..."
Having introduced this [in Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14], the text negates all worldly transactions— such as action, agent, and fruit—

for the wise man; whereas for the ignorant man, who is the opposite of that, the Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa, after stating "for where there is, as it were, duality" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14), demonstrates the very nature of saṃsāra consisting of action, agent, and fruit.

Likewise here too, having withdrawn that fruit which consists of objects characterized by hunger and so forth—the domain of transmigratory existence—[the scripture] proceeds with the thought: "I shall teach for the sake of immortality the knowledge whose object is the sole reality that is the Self of all.
For it is only the ignorant person who is bound by debts regarding the attainment of the worlds of men, ancestors, and gods, not the knower.
This is because of the scriptural injunction regarding the means for attaining the three worlds, such as: "Thus this world of men is [fulfilled] only through a son" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.16);
and because the absence of the obligation of debts is shown for the knower who seeks the world of the Self, by such passages as: "What shall we do with offspring? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
Likewise: "Knowing this, indeed, the Ṛṣis, the Kāvaṣeyas, said thus," and so forth;
and among the Kauṣītakins: "Knowing this, indeed, those of old did not offer the Agnihotra" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 2.5).

If it is argued that, for one who is ignorant, renunciation (pārivrājya) is impossible because he has not discharged his debts, we say no; for the status of being a debtor cannot exist prior to entering the householder stage.

Furthermore, it would follow as an undesirable consequence that even one who has not yet ascended to the [specific] qualification would be a debtor, implying that everyone—even one who has not entered the householder stage—is a debtor [simply by being born], according to the injunction: "Having become a forest-dweller from the home... and so forth.
"Or otherwise, one may renounce even from the stage of studentship (brahmacarya), or from the householder's life, or from the forest-dweller's life" (Jābāla Upaniṣad 4).
Thus, the state of wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya) is indeed accepted as a means for achieving the vision of the Self.
Scriptural injunctions such as "as long as life lasts" (yāvaj-jīvam) find their fulfillment in the case of those who are ignorant but desirous of liberation.
Moreover, in the Chāndogya, it is heard that some, having performed the Agnihotra for twelve nights, thereafter renounce it;
as for the claim that wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya) is intended only for those who are not qualified [for Vedic rites],
that is not so.
For them, these are indeed distinct,
because of scriptural statements such as, "one whose sacred fires have been extinguished, or one who is without fires," and so forth;
moreover, in all the Smṛtis, both the option between the stages of life (āśrama) and their combination are well-established without distinction.
As for the claim that since renunciation is obtained as a matter of course for the wise, it is not the subject of the scripture,

and therefore there is no distinction between one who stays at home or in the forest— that is incorrect; because renunciation itself is what is obtained as a matter of course, there could be no staying elsewhere.
For we have already stated that abiding elsewhere is impelled by desire and action, and that emergence is merely the absence of those two; however,
acting according to one's own will is absolutely unattainable for the knower, since it is understood to pertain exclusively to the utterly deluded.
Likewise, even action enjoined by the scriptures is understood by the knower of the Self to be a heavy burden because it has not been attained [as his own nature];
how much more so the state of being a mere ritualist, which is caused by extreme lack of discrimination?
For an object perceived through the vision of madness or cataracts does not remain the same once that [vision] has ceased.
This is because that [state] has its cause in the vision of the darkness of insanity.

Therefore, for one who knows the Self, it is established that there is neither the state of acting according to one's whims nor any other duty to be performed, except for rising from [meditative absorption].
As for the statement: "He for whom both knowledge and ignorance exist together" (Īśopaniṣad 11).

Thus, the meaning is not that ignorance exists together with knowledge in one who possesses knowledge; rather, what then is the meaning? It is that these two cannot be connected simultaneously in a single person, just as in the case of a single person regarding mother-of-pearl and the cognition of silver in it.
As it is said: "Knowledge and ignorance are far apart, opposite, and divergent" (KaU 1.2.4).
4) Thus it is said in the *Kaṭhaka*:
"Therefore, when knowledge exists, there is no possibility of ignorance.
[As it is said: "Seek to know Brahman through austerity" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 3.2).

2) From such scriptural passages as these, it follows that austerity (*tapas*) and other means for the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*), as well as ritual action (*karman*) such as service to the teacher, are called "ignorance" (*avidyā*) because they are of the nature of ignorance. By means of that [action], having produced knowledge, one transcends death, which is desire. Then, being free from desire and having abandoned all longings, one attains immortality through the knowledge of Brahman. To demonstrate this meaning, it is said: "Having crossed over death by means of ignorance, one attains immortality by means of knowledge" (Īśa Upaniṣad 11). As for the claim that the entirety of a person's lifespan is occupied solely by ritual action—"Performing actions alone here, one should desire to live a hundred years" (Īśa Upaniṣad 2)—[it is refuted by the above].

Thus, this is resolved by being understood as referring to those who lack knowledge, since otherwise it would be impossible. As for the objection that self-knowledge— even though it will be explained later— is not incompatible with ritual action because it is similar to what was previously stated,
that has already been answered by the distinction between the qualified and unqualified Self.
And we shall demonstrate this further in the subsequent explanation.
Therefore, the following section of the text is commenced for the purpose of revealing the knowledge that sees the Self as consisting of the Brahman which is exclusively inactive:
"In the beginning, indeed, this was the Self alone, one only."
There was nothing else whatsoever that blinked. He thought, "Shall I now create the worlds? (AitU 1.1.1)
The Self—derived from the roots *āp* (to obtain), *at* (to pervade), or *at* (to move)—is supreme, omniscient, omnipotent, and devoid of all worldly attributes such as hunger;
its nature is eternally pure, enlightened, and free; it is unborn, undecaying, immortal, deathless, fearless, and non-dual.
Indeed, this very Self alone existed prior to the creation of the world, though that world is differentiated by the distinctions of name, form, and action.
Is it not the case that he alone is one now? No; how then can it be said that "he was"? Even though he is indeed one now, there is nevertheless a distinction.

Prior to its origination, the world—whose differentiation of name and form (*nāmarūpa*) was undifferentiated, which had become the Self itself, and which was the object of the single word and notion "Self"—now, because its differentiation of name and form has become manifest, is the object of manifold words and notions, yet it remains the object of the single word and notion "Self."
And this is the distinction:
just as foam, prior to its differentiation of name and form from water, is the object of only a single word and concept, namely "water";

but when it becomes differentiated from water by a distinct name and form, then it partakes of multiple words and concepts such as "water" and "foam," while simultaneously continuing to partake of the single word and concept "water" alone.
It is just like that:
there is nothing else whatsoever—not even the slightest thing—whether it be active or inactive, or anything else of a different nature.

Just as for the Sāṃkhyas there is no independent *pradhāna* that does not fall within the category of the Self, and just as for the followers of Kaṇāda there are no atoms [that exist apart from it], so too here no other entity whatsoever exists apart from the Self. What then?
The intention is that there was only the Self alone.
Being by nature omniscient, that Self, though being one alone, reflected. Now, an objection may be raised: since prior to creation it lacked a body and sense organs, how could it have reflected?

This is not a fault, because [the Lord] possesses the nature of omniscience; and thus says a Vedic mantra: "Without hands or feet, He is swift and a grasper" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.19), and so forth.
With what intention [does He create]? He says: "I shall create, I shall create the worlds—water and the rest—which serve as the places for living beings to experience the fruits of their karma. //1//
Having thus seen and reflected, he created these worlds: Ambhas, Marīcis, Mara, and Āpas;
"Ambhas" is that which is beyond the sky.
The sky is the foundation;
the intermediate space is the rays;
the earth is the dust.
That which is below is the waters.
He, the Self, created—meaning brought forth—these worlds.

Just as here in this world a wise carpenter or similar craftsman creates palaces and such structures of this kind, so too [the Self] created them immediately after reflecting; having reflected, he creates the palaces and so forth, in that same manner.

Now, one might object: it is logical that a carpenter or similar craftsman creates palaces and such while possessing material causes (*upādāna*), but how can the Self, being without material causes, create the worlds?

This is not a fault; for name-and-form (nāmarūpa), which are like foam upon water, exist as the undifferentiated (avyākṛta) source of the world— which is like differentiated foam— and they constitute its material cause (upādāna), being designated by the single term "Self" (ātman).

Therefore, it is not contradictory that the Omniscient One, being the very substrate for the appropriation of name-and-form which constitute his own self, creates the world. Alternatively, just as a magician possessing consciousness creates himself— as if moving through space— without any material substrate by manifesting himself as another self,
so too it is even more logical that the God who is Omniscient, All-Powerful, and the Great Illusionist (Mahāmāyā) creates himself alone, as another self in the form of the world.
This being the case, the positions of those who maintain that either the effect, the cause, or both are non-existent do not follow as consequences and are thoroughly refuted.

To the question "What worlds did he create?", he says: "Water, mist, vapor, and water. Having produced the cosmic egg through the sequence beginning with space, he created the worlds starting with water.
In this regard, the Śruti itself explains "water" (*ambhas*) and the other terms:
"That world which is beyond the sky—that is, beyond the celestial realm—is called 'water' (*ambhas*);
it is designated by the word 'water' because it sustains (*bharaṇāt*)."
The sky is the foundation and support for that world of water.

Below the celestial realm (dyuloka) is the intermediate space (antarikṣa), which consists of rays of light (marīcyaḥ). Although it is a single entity, it takes the plural form "rays" because it occupies many distinct locations.

Or [it is so called] because of its connection with rays of light (*marīci*). "Earth" (*pṛthivī*) is so called because beings die (*mriyante*) in it; those waters which are below the earth are called *marīcyaḥ*.
From the root *āp* (to obtain), [the word] *lokāḥ* [is derived].
Although the worlds consist of the five elements, nevertheless, because of the predominance of water, they are called by names derived from water: *ambhaḥ*, *marīci*, *mara*, and *āpaḥ*. //2//

Having created the four worlds, which serve as the substratum for the appropriation of the fruits of the karma of all living beings, he reflected: "These worlds now exist; let me create the guardians of the worlds."
He drew forth a person from the waters alone and gave it form.
That Lord reflected again:

"These worlds, beginning with water, which have been created by me, might perish if they are devoid of guardians; therefore, for the sake of their protection, let me create the world-protectors (lokapālas), the guardians of the worlds.

Having reflected thus, he [created them] from the waters—that is, from the five elements, of which water is the primary constituent, from those very same elements from which he had previously created water and the others.

Having extracted from the waters a person in human form, possessing a head, hands, and so forth—just as potters extract a lump of clay from the earth—he consolidated it, that is, he formed it into a mass by joining its own parts together. //3//
He brooded over it;
from it, thus brooded upon, the mouth was cleft open like an egg,
and from the mouth, speech emerged.
From speech, fire was produced;
the two nostrils were cleft open;
from the nostrils, breath was produced.
From the vital breath (prāṇa) came the wind; the two eyes were split open;
from the two eyes came sight.
The sun [emerged] from the eye;
the two ears were split open;
from the two ears, hearing [emerged].
From the ear, the quarters [of space] emerged;
the skin was split open;
from the skin, the body hairs emerged.
From the body hairs, the plants and trees [arose];
the heart was split open;
from the heart, the mind [arose].
From the mind, the moon [was produced];
the navel burst forth;
from the navel, the downward breath (apāna) [was produced].
From the downward breath, death;
the penis was split open;
from the penis, semen.
From semen, water.
He brooded over that mass, intending it for a human form; the meaning is that he performed meditation and formed a volition, as it is said:
"His austerity consists of knowledge" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.9).
9) From such scriptural passages as these:

when that body-mass was heated—meaning heated by austerity through the volition of the Lord (īśvara)—its mouth burst open; an aperture in the form of a mouth was produced, just as the egg of a bird bursts open. From that opened mouth, the organ of speech, the instrument [of action], emerged.
Agni, the guardian of the world, was the presiding deity over that [speech].
Then the two nostrils were split open;
from the nostrils came the vital breath (prāṇa).
The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the wind (*vāyu*);
thus, in every case, the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the deity (*devatā*)—this triad—is sequentially differentiated.
The eyes, ears, skin, and heart are the loci of the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
The mind is the internal organ;
the navel is the seat where all vital breaths are bound.
Because it is conjoined with the apāna breath, the anal faculty is called "apāna."
Therefore, its presiding deity is Death.
Just as elsewhere,
so too the penis was split open, which is the location of the generative organ.
The sense organ is semen; because it exists for the purpose of discharging semen, it is spoken of together with semen.
"From semen, water [arises]. //4//
Thus ends the first section of the first chapter.
//1// These deities, once created, fell into this great ocean.
He afflicted them with hunger and thirst.
They said to him: "Find for us an abode, established in which we may eat food. (AitU 1.2.1)

Having thus conceived these deities, Agni and the others, as the guardians of the worlds, the Lord created them for this great ocean of worldly existence—a sea of saṃsāra originating from ignorance, desire, and karma; one whose waters are suffering, which possesses the fierce crocodiles of disease, old age, and death; which is beginningless, endless, shoreless, and without support; where the momentary rest afforded by the fragments of pleasure born of sense objects and the senses is but a mirage; and which is tossed by hundreds of great waves of calamity arising from the wind of thirst for the objects of the five senses.

In this great ocean, where there is the great roar arising from the cries and lamentations such as "Hā hā! of those who have gone to many hells beginning with Mahāraurava; where the boat of knowledge is filled with the provisions for the journey consisting of truth, integrity, generosity, compassion, non-violence, tranquility, self-restraint, fortitude, and other personal virtues; and which has the path of association with the virtuous and total renunciation as its way, and liberation as its shore—into this [ocean], they have fallen, as it were.

Therefore, even that goal described as characterized by the merging into deities such as Fire, which is the fruit of practicing the combination of knowledge and action, is not sufficient for the cessation of the suffering of saṃsāra.

This is the intended meaning here. Since this is so, therefore, having understood thus, the Supreme Brahman— which is the Self of oneself and of all beings, which possesses the qualifications to be described,
and which is the subject under discussion as the cause of the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of the world— must be known for the sake of pacifying all the sufferings of saṃsāra.

Therefore, this knowledge of the Supreme Brahman as the Self is "this path, this deed, this Brahman, this truth" (AiU 2.1.1), according to the Vedic mantra: "There is no other path for going" (ŚvetU 3.8; MuU 6.15).

He directed—that is, led toward and joined with—hunger and thirst that first-created Person, who was the mass [of the body] and the seed-source of the deities of the places and organs. Because that causal source possessed defects such as hunger and thirst, the deities who were its effects also possessed hunger and thirst.
Then, being afflicted by hunger and thirst, they said to this Grandfather, the Creator: "Provide for us, ordain a dwelling place—a locus—for us."
"In which sphere established, we true ones are capable of eating—that is, consuming—food? (1)
When this was said, Īśvara brought a cow to them;
they said, "Indeed, this one is not sufficient for us."
He brought a horse for them; they said, "This one is certainly not enough for us. (AitU 1.2.2)
From those deities, he took a ball of food distinguished by the form of a cow and, having extracted a ball from those very waters as before and kneaded it, he brought it and showed it to them.

When they saw the form of the cow, they said: "Indeed, this ball is not sufficient for us; it is not enough for our purpose, that is, for the sake of a physical basis [to dwell upon] and for eating. It is not sufficient—meaning it is not adequate or fit to be eaten."
When the cow was refused, he brought a horse for them; they said, "This one is certainly not enough for us," as before.
When everything had been rejected,
he brought a man to them;
they said, "Ah, well done!"
"The person, indeed, is the well-done.
He said to them, "Enter according to your respective abodes. (AitU 1.2.3)
He brought a man from them who was their own source.

Seeing the man, who was their own source, they said, "Truly, this foundation has been well-made, it is beautiful! Therefore, the man (*puruṣa*) is indeed called "well-made" (*sukṛta*); he is so called because he is the cause of all meritorious deeds, or because he is made by himself through his own self and his own powers of illusion (*māyā*).
The Lord said to those deities, "This is the sacrificial offering for you; this is your abode," thinking that all beings indeed delight in their own source.
Therefore, enter each according to its proper station—that is, enter whatever station is suitable for each one's function, such as speaking and so forth. //3//
Having obtained the permission of the Lord with the words "So be it," just as the military commanders and others do in a city—
fire, becoming speech, entered the mouth;
wind, becoming breath, entered the nostrils.
The sun, having become the eye, entered the eyes;
the quarters of space, having become the ear, entered the ears;
the plants and trees, having become the body hairs, entered the skin.
The moon, having become the mind, entered the heart;
death, having become the out-breath (apāna), entered the navel;
the waters, having become semen, entered the generative organ. (AitU 1.2.4)
Agni, the presiding deity of speech, having become speech itself, entered his own source, the mouth; the rest is as previously explained.
Vāyu entered the nostrils, Āditya the eyes, the quarters the ears, the herbs and forests the skin, the Moon the heart, Mṛtyu the navel, and the Waters the generative organ. 4.
When the deities had thus received their empowerment, Hunger and Thirst said to him, "Recognize us.
He replied to them, "I shall grant you a share in these very deities; I shall make you their co-sharers."
Therefore, for whatever deity the oblation is taken, hunger and thirst become its co-sharers.
When truth (satya) was without a substratum, hunger and thirst said to that Lord:
"Consider for us a substratum; think it out; provide one"—this is the meaning.
Being thus addressed, that Lord spoke to those two, hunger and thirst.
For since you two are of the nature of existence (*bhāvarūpa*), your status as agents is not possible without depending upon a conscious entity.
Therefore, among these very deities—Agni and the others—who are both the *adhyātma* and *adhidaivata*, I share with you both; that is, I favor you by means of a distribution of your functions.
Among these, whatever portion consisting of oblations and the like belongs to whichever deity, it shall belong to her alone by that very [means].
"I make you two sharers by means of a share, or possessors of a share.

Because the Lord (Īśvara) ordained this at the beginning of creation, therefore even now, for whichever deity an oblation—characterized as cooked rice, sacrificial cake, and so forth—is taken, hunger and thirst become sharers and possessors of a share in that very deity. 5.
Thus ends the second section of the first chapter.
He reflected: "Now here are these worlds and the guardians of the worlds;
let me create food for them. (AitU 1.3.1)
For thus in the world, the independence of lords over their own favor and punishment is observed;
likewise, because Maheśvara is the Lord of all, he possesses absolute independence even in the punishment and favor of all beings. //1//
He brooded over the waters.
From those waters thus brooded upon, a form was born.
That form which was born is indeed food. (Aitareya Upaniṣad 1.3.2)
That Lord, desiring to create food, brooded over those very waters mentioned previously.
From them, thus brooded upon as the material cause, there was born—produced—the "embodied," that is, the solid form capable of supporting things, characterized by the moving and the non-moving.
That which was born as the embodied form is indeed food. 2.
Once it was created, it sought to flee away;
he desired to seize it with speech,
but he was not able to seize it with speech.
If he had grasped it by means of speech alone, he would have satisfied himself with food merely by uttering it.

Thus, this food was created facing [the eater] for the sake of the worlds and the world-protectors; just as a mouse or similar creature, perceiving "this is my death, the devourer of food," flees away— meaning it turns its back and desires to go beyond those who would eat it, beginning to run away— the aggregate of the worlds and world-protectors, characterized by the body and its organs, being the first-born and seeing no other devourers of food, desired to seize that food through speech, by means of the activity of speaking.
He desired to grasp that food; however, he was unable, nor was he capable, of grasping or taking it up by means of speech—that is, by the act of speaking.

If that first-born embodied being had grasped this food by means of speech—if he had taken it up—then everyone in the world would have become satisfied after merely uttering it, because [the food] would have been its effect.
But this is not the case;
therefore, we understand that even the progenitor was unable to grasp it with speech. //3//
The subsequent [passage] is the same:
He sought to grasp it with breath;
he was not able to grasp it with breath.
If he had grasped that food with the out-breath alone, one would have to swallow food after merely breathing out.
He desired to grasp it with the eye;
he was not able to grasp it with the eye. Had he been able to grasp it with the eye, one would have been satisfied merely by seeing food. (AitU 1.3.5)
He desired to grasp it with the ear. He was not able to grasp it with the ear.
Had he grasped it with the ear, one would have been satisfied by merely hearing the food. (AitU 1.3.6)
He sought to grasp it with the skin;
he was not able to grasp it with the skin.
Had he grasped it with the skin, he would have been satisfied by merely touching food.
He desired to grasp it with the mind. He was not able to grasp it with the mind. Had he grasped it with the mind, one would have satisfied oneself on food merely by thinking of it. (AitU 1.3.8)
He sought to grasp it with the penis;
he was not able to grasp it with the penis.
Had he grasped it with the penis, he would have released his food and perished from hunger. (AitU 1.3.9)
He sought to grasp it with the out-breath; he swallowed it. This wind is the seizer of food.
Vāyu, indeed, is life-breath.

Being unable to grasp that food by means of that breath, that eye, that ear, that skin, that mind, or that organ of generation— by each of those respective functions of the senses— he subsequently desired to seize that food through the downward-moving wind (apāna) via the opening of the mouth;
then he ate it, having thus grasped and consumed that very food.
Therefore, this very downward-moving air (apānavāyu) is the "seizer" (graha) of food, meaning it is the grasper of food.
Or rather, that which is the air is the life-force of food, the bond of food, and the sustainer of food; indeed, it is well known that this very air is such. 4-10.
He reflected: "How indeed might this be without me? He reflected: "By which way shall I enter?
He reflected: "Whether it be what is uttered by speech, or what is breathed by the breath, or what is seen by the eye, or what is heard by the ear..."
"If it was heard by the ear, or touched by the skin, or meditated upon by the mind, or inhaled by the breath, or emitted by the organ of generation—then who am I? (AitU 1.3.11)

Having thus established the existence of the world, its guardians, and their assembly as being dependent upon a cause, he, like a lord, observed the stability of the city, its citizens, and its protectors—pondering in what manner and by what means this might be so. He reflected:
"How indeed, without me—the master of the city—could this body, which is a composite of organs and faculties to be described hereafter, exist for the sake of another, were it not for me?"

If speech were merely the act of vocal utterance and so forth, it would be entirely useless in no way whatsoever, like the praise offered to a guest; for just as that praise, when employed by bards and others for the sake of a master, would not exist at all in the absence of a master, so too [would speech].

Therefore, there must be a supreme master who presides over it, acting as the witness to the fruits of what is done and not done, and as the enjoyer—just as a king [is the witness and enjoyer] of a city.

If indeed this state of being for the sake of another—which belongs to the aggregate of effects—were to exist without me, a conscious being who seeks that other's purpose, just as the business of a city and its citizens exists for the sake of their master;
then who am I, what is my nature, or whose master am I?
For if I did not enter into this aggregate of causes and effects, I would not perceive the results such as speech and utterance, just like a king [who does not see his own work].

Having entered the city, he would oversee what has been done and what has not been done by the appointed officials, so that no one might recognize or reflect upon him, thinking, "This person who is thus constituted is me.
Conversely, however, he should think: "He who knows this as 'this' through the articulation of speech and so forth—may I become such that I am recognized as being of the nature of that knowledge."
"For the sake of what purpose is there this speech and so forth of these [organs] joined together?
Just as pillars, walls, and other such components, when joined together in a palace or similar structure, exist for the sake of another who is not themselves joined [in that way], so it is here.
Having thus reflected, [the text asks]: "Therefore, by which [path] shall I proceed?"
The soles of the feet and the head are the two entry paths for this aggregate;
by which of these two paths shall I enter this city characterized as an aggregate of body and organs? //11//
Having observed this, [the Self] did not enter by way of the feet—the path of entry for my servant Prāṇa, who is authorized over all matters;
rather, by process of elimination, thinking "I shall enter by splitting open his head," it acted like a person who does what has been observed:
"He split open that very suture and entered through that door."
This very door is called the "Opening" (vidṛti). This is the "Delightful Place" (nāndana).
It has three dwelling-places, three states of sleep: "This is a dwelling-place, this is a dwelling-place, this is a dwelling-place. (AitUp 1.3.12)

That Lord of the Sacrifice, having split open this very suture of the head—the limit of the parting of the hair—and having made it perforated, entered and penetrated this world, which is the aggregate of causes and effects, by means of that door and path. For this is the well-known door, since when oil and such are poured upon the head, one perceives their essence and so forth within; this very opening is known as "Vidṛti" (the Split) because it has been split open. It is the well-known door.

But the other doors, such as those of the ear and so forth, are not "prosperous" (samṛddhi) nor causes of bliss, because they are common paths like those used by servants and others. This door, however, belongs to the Supreme Lord alone; therefore, this is truly "Nāndana," that which causes delight. The form "nāndanam" is a Vedic archaism for "nandanam"; one rejoices by going through this door into the supreme Brahman.
For him who has thus created [the body] and entered it by means of the living self (jīva-ātman), like a king entering his city, there are three abodes:
the place of the senses during the waking state—namely, the right eye; the internal mind at the time of dreaming;
and the space within the heart at the time of deep sleep. This is so.
Or, there are three states to be described hereafter: the father’s body, the mother’s womb, and one’s own body.
There are three dreams, known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
Now, one might object that the waking state is not a dream, because its nature is that of full consciousness.
It is not so; it is merely a dream.
Why? Because there is an absence of awakening to one's own ultimate self, and because one perceives unreal objects just as in a dream.
This very dwelling has the right eye as its first [entrance].
The mind is the second [abode], and the space within the heart is the third;
this is merely a restatement of what was called "the dwelling place."
For within those dwellings, existing by turns as their own physical bodies, they remain in a state of deep sleep for a long time due to ignorance;
they do not awaken even through the blows of the mallets of suffering born from the convergence of many hundreds of thousands of calamities, which are innate to them. (12)
Once born, he looked out upon all beings, thinking, "What else here is there that I might speak?
He beheld this very Person as the most pervasive Brahman, [thinking], "I have seen this. 3.13.13.

Once born, having entered the body as the individual self (*jīvātman*), he manifested and differentiated the elements. At one time, when the great drum of the Vedāntic Mahāvākyas— which awakens the knowledge of the Self— was being struck at the root of his ear by a supremely compassionate teacher, [he perceived] this very Person under discussion, the agent of creation and so forth, as the Self dwelling within the city (*puri*).

"Brahma" consists of the syllable *bṛhat*, which is the greatest; by the single elision of the letter *ta*, it becomes "tata," meaning most pervasive, most all-encompassing, and perfectly full like space. He realized—that is, he perceived—how? "This Brahma is my own self;
I have seen its true nature. Thus he saw.
"Aho" [is used] with a protracted vowel (*pluti*) for the purpose of deliberation, as previously stated in Pāṇini 8.2.103.
Because he saw that Brahman— which is immediate and direct, the innermost of all— as "this" (idam) rather than through indirect means,
therefore his name is Idandra;
indeed, his name is Idandra.
Although he is this very Indra, they call him "Indra" by means of a cryptic name;
for the gods, as it were, love what is cryptic—yes, the gods, as it were, love what is cryptic. (AitU 1.3.14)
Therefore, because he sees this, the Supreme Self is named *Idandra*.

Indeed, the Lord is well-known in the world by the name *Idandra*. Since he is thus *Idandra*, those who know Brahman call him "Indra" by means of an indirect expression for the sake of conventional usage.
Because he is most worthy of worship, and out of fear of pronouncing his name directly— since the gods, as it were, prefer what is indirect and are fond of having their names mentioned indirectly—
how much more so Maheśvara, who is the god even of all the gods?
The dual number is for the purpose of concluding the present chapter. //14//
Thus ends the third section of the first chapter. //3//

In this fourth chapter, the first section of the second book, the meaning of the sentence is as follows: [Brahman] is the creator of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of the world, is non-transmigratory, and is omniscient.

The All-powerful One, the Knower of All, having created this entire world out of Himself alone—without employing any other material cause—in the sequence beginning with space, entered of His own accord all bodies possessed of life-breath and so forth for the sake of awakening to His own Self.
Having entered, He directly realized His own Self, thinking: "I am this very Brahman, which is immortal."
Therefore, that very Self alone is one and the same in all bodies, and there is no other.
Furthermore, [the scripture says]: "One should know: 'The Self is equal; I am Brahman. And:
"In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1)

Thus it has been said, "Brahman is all-pervading" (1.3.13), and elsewhere as well: "For that which is omnipresent and the Self of all, there is not even a space the size of the tip of a hair that has not been entered. How then could it have entered by splitting open a boundary, like an ant entering a hole?
Is this not indeed a very slight objection? Much more ought to be challenged here: being himself uncreated, he looked on; without depending on anything else, he created the worlds.

Having extracted the Puruṣa from the waters, he gave him form. From his meditating upon that, the mouth and other organs were manifested; from the mouth and other organs, the world-protectors such as Agni and others emerged. Then followed their connection with hunger, thirst, and so forth, their longing for a dwelling place, the presentation of cows and other things for that purpose, their entry into those respective dwellings, and [the creation] of the food for them.
Or [the opponent might argue that] fleeing by means of speech and so forth is due to a desire to seize that [object]; all of this is equivalent to breaking through a boundary and entering.
Well then, let all of this be untenable.

No; since here only the realization of the Self is intended, there is no fault, as this entire [narrative] is a figurative explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). Or rather, the more reasonable position is that the omniscient and omnipotent Lord, like a master illusionist, performed all this through the expansion of narratives and so forth, in the manner of worldly stories, for the sake of easy understanding and comprehension.
For no fruit whatsoever is intended from the thorough knowledge of accounts such as the creation myth;
rather, the fruit of immortality is well-established in all the Upaniṣads as resulting from the thorough knowledge of the nature of the one Self (aikātmya).
And in the Smṛtis, such as the Gītā and others, this is stated in passages beginning with: “The Supreme Lord abides equally in all beings” (Gītā 13.27).
Is it not the case that there are three selves?
One is the *jīva*, the enjoyer, the agent, and the transmigrator, which is well-known in all the world and its scriptures.

[The other two are] indicated by the sign of the creation of worlds and bodies—which serve as multiple substrates capable of experiencing the fruits of the karma of numerous living beings—in accordance with what is demonstrated in the scriptures.

By the evidence of the construction of cities, palaces, and so forth, it is understood that there exists a creator of those things who possesses knowledge of skill regarding them—just as a carpenter or similar artisan—and thus the Lord, the omniscient creator of the universe, is known as a second conscious Self.
[As it is said: "From whence words turn back" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4).

1) "Not this, not this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26)—the person established by such scriptural passages is the third, the one known from the Upaniṣads. Thus, these three selves are mutually distinct. In that case, how can it be known that there is only one self, non-dual and free from saṃsāra?
To understand this, first, how is the individual soul (jīva) itself to be known?
Indeed, it is thus known that [the Self] is the hearer, the thinker, the seer, the director, the proclaimer, the knower, and the perceiver.

But is this not a contradiction, for it is known that He who is the agent of hearing and so forth is "not thought" (amata), yet is also "thought" (mata), and "not known" (avijñāta), yet is also "known" (vijñāta)?
Likewise, there are such passages as: “Do not seek the thinker of thinking; do not seek to know the knower of knowing” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.2). And so forth.
This is true, yet it is contradictory, if [the Self] were known through direct perception like pleasure and so forth;
for direct perceptual knowledge is precluded by such passages as, "You should not think of the thinker of thought" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.2).
But it is known through the indicative marks of hearing and so forth; in that case, how can there be a contradiction?
[Objection: But even by the indicative marks of hearing and so forth, how is it known?

To the extent that when the self hears a sound that is to be heard, at that time, because its activity consists solely in hearing, the activities of reflecting and cognizing are not possible— whether with respect to itself or another—
and this is likewise the case for other activities such as reflection; furthermore,
activities such as hearing occur only with respect to their own respective objects.
For the act of thinking cannot occur apart from the thinker and that which is to be thought.
[Objection: Is it not the case that everything is indeed to be thought by means of the mind?
[Reply: True, it is so; nevertheless, even though everything is to be thought, it is impossible to think anything without a thinker.
If that were so, what would follow? This would be the consequence here:
whoever is this thinker of everything, being merely a thinker, he would not be an object of thought.
Furthermore, there is no second thinker who thinks [of the self].
When it must be thought of by itself, then both that by which the self is to be thought—the self as subject—and that which is to be thought—the self as object—would follow as two distinct entities.
The single self would thus split into two parts, like a bamboo stalk, by virtue of being both the thinker and the object of thought; however, neither of these possibilities is tenable.
Just as it is impossible for two lamps to stand in the relationship of the illuminated and the illuminator due to their equality, so it is here.
Furthermore, there is no time devoid of the activity of thinking when the thinker thinks of the object of thought for the sake of self-reflection;
even when the thinker thinks of the self by means of an inferential mark (liṅga), [it is not free from that activity].
Even then, the self must be inferred by means of a mark (liṅga) as before; thus, there would result two [entities]: the one who infers and that which is inferred.
Or else, [the self] being one, it would be twofold—this is the previously mentioned fault.
If it is not known through perception nor through inference, how can it be said: “One should know: ‘That is my self’” (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.8)?
9) Thus [you ask]: "How can there be a hearer or a thinker, and so forth?
Is it not the case that the self possesses attributes such as being a hearer, and that the absence of hearing and so forth is well-established for the self?
What do you see as inconsistent in this?
Although this is not problematic for you, it nevertheless appears problematic to me.
How so? When that person is a hearer, he is not a thinker; when he is a thinker, he is not a hearer.
This being the case, according to your position, he is a hearer and a thinker at one time, yet at another time he is neither a hearer nor a thinker.
Likewise, it is stated elsewhere:

"When this is so, then how is there no inconsistency for you in a state of doubt as to whether the self possesses the property of being a hearer and so forth, or possesses the property of not being a hearer and so forth?
When Devadatta goes, at that time he is not a stationary one, but a goer indeed."
When one stands, at that time one is not a goer, but is simply a stander;
thus, in this position, there is both going and standing,
but not a permanent state of either going or standing.
In the same way,
the followers of Kaṇāda and others perceive it here;
for the Self is described by means of attributes such as hearing that are applicable to it, based on statements such as "the hearer," "the thinker," and so forth.
For they declare that cognition arises from conjunction and is not simultaneous;
they demonstrate this by saying, "My mind was elsewhere, I did not see," and so forth. And it is logical that the non-arising of cognitions simultaneously is the mark (*liṅga*) of the mind.
Let it be so; what is lost to you if it were thus?
Let it be as you desire, if that is your wish;
however, the meaning of the scripture is not possible [in that way].
Is it not the meaning of such scriptural passages as "He is neither the hearer nor the thinker"?
No, because of statements such as "neither hearer nor thinker.
But have you not already answered this by [stating that the former] is merely a conditional (pākṣika) view?
No, because the capacity for hearing and so forth is admitted to be eternal,
according to such scriptural passages as: "For there is no loss of the hearing of the hearer" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.27).

If that were the case, then by accepting that the self is eternally a hearer and so forth, the simultaneous arising of cognitions—which contradicts direct perception—would have to be postulated as being due to the absence of non-cognition in the self;
and that is undesirable. Thus, neither of the two faults arises.
Because scripture and other sources declare that the Self possesses attributes such as being a hearer;
whereas the eyes and other organs, which are impermanent and material, possess vision and other functions that are likewise impermanent, characterized by conjunction and disjunction—
just as the flaming of fire arises from its conjunction with grass and other fuels.

However, it is not possible for that which is eternal, formless, and characterized by the absence of conjunction and disjunction to possess impermanent attributes such as vision produced by conjunction;
thus says the Śruti: “For there is no loss of the vision of the seer” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23), and so forth.
If this is so, then there are two kinds of vision: the impermanent vision of the eye and the eternal vision of the Self.
And thus there are two kinds of hearing for the sense of hearing: the non-eternal, which belongs to the ear, and the eternal, which belongs to the nature of the Self.

Likewise, there are two kinds of cognition: the external, which is discriminative, and the internal. For it is exactly so; and thus this scriptural passage becomes consistent: "The seer of seeing, the hearer of hearing," and so forth.

The world also commonly recognizes that when cataracts (timira) come and go for the eye, one says, "vision was lost" or "vision has arisen," thus establishing the impermanence of visual perception; likewise, the permanence of hearing, memory, and so forth, as well as the self-perception and other such faculties, is indeed well-established in the world.
For one whose eyes have been plucked out says in a dream, "Today I saw my brother."
Likewise, for one who has understood [the nature of] deafness, a mantra heard in a dream today and so forth [would not be remembered].
If the self’s eternal vision were produced by conjunction with the eye, then upon its destruction, that vision would perish;
consequently, one whose eyes have been removed would not perceive blue, yellow, and so forth, even in a dream.
Furthermore, scriptural passages such as, “For the seer is not the seeing” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23), and “That eye is the person by which one sees in a dream,” would otherwise be untenable.
The view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is eternal and grasps at the view of external impermanence.

Since the external view possesses impermanent characteristics such as arising and passing away, it is logical that the view of a self which grasps it appears as such; thus, impermanence and so forth are the causes of delusion for the world.
This is just as the perception of an object such as a whirling firebrand—which possesses the property of rotation—also appears as if it were itself spinning.
And thus says the Śruti: "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7).
Therefore, because the vision of the Self is eternal, there is neither simultaneity nor non-simultaneity.

However, due to the influence of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of external, non-eternal perceptions—and because both common people and logicians are devoid of the traditional transmission of the scriptures—the delusion that the vision of the Self is non-eternal is indeed logically established.
The conceptualization of distinctions between the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśvara), and the Supreme Self (paramātman) is caused by this very [ignorance].

Likewise, whatever dualities of speech and mind there may be—such as "it exists" or "it does not exist"—they become one in that which is the object of the eternal vision, the undifferentiated [Reality]; regarding that, [the notions] "it exists" or "it does not exist,"...
One is manifold;
it possesses qualities and lacks qualities;
it knows and it does not know.
It possesses action yet is without action; it possesses fruit yet is without fruit; it has a seed yet is seedless;
it is pleasure and it is pain.
Whoever wishes to conceptualize that which is beyond the range of words and cognitions— whether as "middling-middling," "empty" or "non-empty," or as "I," "the other," or "another"— [is mistaken].
He surely wishes to wrap the sky like a piece of leather, to climb a staircase with his feet, and he desires to see the tracks of fish in the water and of birds in the sky.
"Not this, not this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26).
23) From such scriptural passages as, "From which words turn back" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1),
and "Who indeed knows? (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.3).
6) From such scriptural passages as these [mantras].
How then is there the realization for him that "That is my Self"?
Tell me, in what manner may I know that "I am That, That is my Self"?
Regarding this, they relate a story: it is said that a certain foolish man was told by some people, upon the occurrence of a certain offense, "Shame on you! You are not a human being.
Out of his foolishness, he approached someone else in order to prove his own humanity and said, "Please tell me, who am I?
Knowing his foolishness, the other man replied:
"I shall instruct you gradually," he said;
then, having set aside his physical form as a stationary being and so forth, he ceased speaking, saying, "You are not a non-human.
Being thus bewildered, he replied to him: "You began to instruct me, yet you have become silent."
Why does it not cause awakening?
Such is the nature of that speech.

For how could one who, even when told "you are no non-human," does not realize his own humanity, ever realize his own humanity even when told "you are a human"? Therefore, [one must proceed] according to the instruction of the treatise.
This alone is the method for realizing the Self; there is no other.
For indeed, grass or any other combustible material cannot be burned by fire through anything else.
Therefore, the scripture, being intent on making known the true nature of the Self, proceeds by means of the negation of non-humanity, saying, "Not this, not this."
Having said this, [the teacher] ceased.
Likewise: "Without interior or exterior" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19;
3.8.8); "This Self is Brahman, the experiencer of all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2...).
5–19) Such is the instruction:
“That thou art” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.8.16);
“But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14; 4.5.15).
15) And also [the passage] beginning with "Thus, etc.

means that as long as this [individual] does not know this very Self as it has been described, so long does he, having accepted through ignorance an external limiting adjunct characterized by the view of impermanence as being the Self, and imagining the attributes of that adjunct to belong to the Self, [transmigrates] among the states of gods, animals, and humans, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
Returning again and again, one wanders through the cycle of existence under the power of ignorance, desire, and karma.

Thus proceeding in this very manner—like the current of a river, with the continuity of birth and death remaining unbroken—the Śruti speaks to demonstrate by means of which states one exists, for the purpose of generating dispassion: "Verily, O Puruṣa, from the very beginning this person becomes an embryo, namely, this semen."
This radiance, having been produced from all his limbs, sustains itself within himself.
When he pours it into a woman, then he procreates it;
that is his first birth. (AitUp 2.1)

This very transmigrating soul, possessed of ignorance, desire, action, and egoism, having performed sacrifices and other rites, departs from this world through the sequence of smoke and so forth, and becomes food. It is offered as an oblation into the fire of the person; and in that person, indeed, this transmigrating soul first of all—beginning from the very start—becomes an embryo in the form of semen. This is what is meant by the phrase, "in the form of that which is the semen in the person. And this semen is the essence of the body, consisting of the vital energy (*tejas*) produced and perfected from all the limbs and parts of the body characterized by the sapids and so forth; because it constitutes the very self of the person, it is called the "Self" (*ātman*).
He bears—that is, he sustains—that very Self within himself, that is, within his own body, in the form of semen once it has become an embryo.

When, at which time, the wife is in her season, he pours that semen into the fire of the woman as he approaches her; then, at that moment, the father generates this very semen, which has become the embryo of his own self.
The departure of this person from that place at the time of the emission of semen is the first birth, the manifestation of the first state, of this transmigrating being in the form of semen.
This has been stated previously in the passage beginning with, "That Self [entered] into that Self," and so forth. //1//
It becomes the very self of that woman, just like her own limb;
therefore, it does not harm her.
She perceives this self of his as having entered into her here. (AitU 2.2)

That semen, when discharged into a woman, attains the state of being her very self—that is, non-difference from her self—just as it does for the father; it reaches that state just as one's own limbs, such as the breasts, do.
For this reason, that embryo does not harm this mother, as a carbuncle or the like might.
Since it has become her very self, like her own limbs such as the breasts, it therefore does not harm or afflict her; this is the meaning.

Being pregnant, she—realizing that this self of her husband had entered and gone into the interior of her own self—nourishes, develops, and protects [the fetus], avoiding food and other things incompatible with the embryo while employing suitable food and so forth. //2//
She becomes the one who brings [him] forth and that which is to be brought forth;
she, the woman, bears that embryo,
and he, from the very beginning, brings the boy into being even prior to birth.
When he contemplates the boy at the beginning of his birth, he thereby contemplates his own self for the continuity of these worlds;
for thus are these worlds continuous.
That is his second birth. (AitUp 2.3)
She is the nourisher and the fosterer of her husband, who was her own embryo; she is to be nourished, fostered, and protected by him, for he becomes her husband.
Indeed, in this world, no relationship between anyone and anything is tenable without mutual benefit and counter-benefit.
That woman bears and carries that embryo according to the prescribed method of gestation prior to birth.
That father, at the very beginning— indeed immediately after birth— nurtures the newborn boy with the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) and other ceremonies.
Since that father nurtures the boy with the birth-rite and so forth at the very outset, immediately after birth,
he thereby nurtures his own self.
For the father himself is indeed born in the form of a son;

thus it has been said: "The husband enters the wife" (Hari-vamśa 3.73.31), and so forth. Why then is it said that he brings himself into being by generating [himself] in the form of a son? The meaning is: for the sake of the continuity and non-interruption of these worlds.
These worlds would indeed perish if no one were to perform such acts as the procreation of offspring;

for it is because these worlds continue to exist in an unbroken succession through the uninterrupted performance of duties like procreation that they persist. Therefore, the meaning is that this must be done for the sake of preventing their cessation, not for the sake of liberation.

Thus, for this transmigrating being, the emergence from the mother's womb in the form of a child is the second birth, the manifestation of a second state, when considered in relation to its prior form as semen. //3//
Thus, this self of his is assigned to meritorious deeds;
then that other self of his, having accomplished its purpose and reached the end of its lifespan, departs.
As soon as it departs from here, it is born again.
That is his third birth. (AitUp 2.4)

This son is the very self of this father; he is established for the sake of performing the meritorious actions prescribed in the scriptures, in order to accomplish those duties. The meaning is that he is appointed as a representative in the place of the father to perform whatever must be done by the father.
Thus, in the *Vājasaneyaka*, regarding the knowledge of succession (*saṃpratti-vidyā*), one instructed by the father says: "I am Brahman, I am the sacrifice" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.17).
17) "Thus he practices," and so forth.

Immediately thereafter, having entrusted his own burden to his son—meaning that this other person, the father, has fulfilled his duty and is liberated from the three debts (*ṛṇatraya*), having accomplished what was to be done—and being advanced in years, having reached old age and become decrepit, he departs; that is, he dies.

Departing from here, even while abandoning this very body, he takes up another body like a caterpillar moving to another blade of grass; thus, accumulated by his karma, he is born again. That which is to be attained by him after death is his third birth. But is it not the case that for one transmigrating, the first birth occurs from the father in the form of semen?
It is stated that his second birth was in the form of a youth as the son of his mother;
when his third birth is to be described, why is it said that the birth of the father as a *preta* is the third?
This is not a fault, because the intended meaning is the essential identity (*aikātmya*) between father and son.

That son also, having placed the burden upon his own son, departs from here and is born again just like his father. Regarding this, it is considered by the Śruti that what is stated in one place applies equally elsewhere, because of the single selfhood of father and son. //4//

Thus, as all the world wanders through the cycle of birth and death, mounted upon the continuity of existence by means of the three manifestations of the states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep], it falls into the great ocean of *saṃsāra*.

Yet, whenever— be it in any state whatsoever— one realizes the Self as declared in the Śruti, at that very moment one becomes liberated from all the bonds of *saṃsāra* and has accomplished all that was to be done.
This was said by the Seer: "While still in the womb, I indeed knew all these births of the gods;
a hundred iron fortresses guarded me, but then I flew out with the speed of a hawk.
Thus it is said.
While still lying within the womb, Vāmadeva spoke thus. (AitU 2.5)
He says that this matter was also stated by the Seer in a mantra:
"While still in the mother's womb, in the very uterus of the womb"—
the particle *nu* expresses deliberation (*vitarke*).

The meaning is: "Aho! By the power of the ripening of meditations (*bhāvanā*) through many previous births, I have known—indeed, I have fully awakened to—all the births, that is, all the various births, of these gods, Agni and the others. "A hundred"—meaning many—"iron forts" (*purā āyasīḥ*); the intention is that they are bodies as if made of iron, impenetrable.

They did not protect me—that is, they failed to guard me from falling downward by escaping the snares of *saṃsāra*. Then, like a hawk breaking through a net, I emerged (*niradīyam*) with speed, having attained the power produced by self-knowledge (*ātma-jñāna*).
"Aha! Even while lying in the womb," the seer Vāmadeva spoke thus. (5)
He, knowing thus, having ascended upwards after the dissolution of this body, having attained all desires in that heavenly world, became immortal—he became immortal. (AitUp 2.6)

That seer Vāmadeva, knowing the Self exactly as it has been described, [is liberated] upon the dissolution of this body— the body which is imagined through ignorance, which is like iron in its indestructibility, and which is a continuous succession of bodies entered by hundreds of manifold evils such as birth, death, and old age— due to the destruction of that body, which means due to the eradication of the causes of the seed for the production of the body, namely ignorance and so forth, by the power produced from the consumption of the nectar of the knowledge of the Supreme Self.

Having become the Supreme Self, having ascended above the downward-flowing cycle of transmigratory existence, and having attained the stainless state of being the Self of all as illumined by knowledge, he reached— like a lamp— the extinction (*nirvāṇa*) in this aforementioned world of heaven, which is undecaying, immortal, deathless, fearless, omniscient, without prior or posterior, without interior or exterior, and whose sole essence is the nectar of wisdom; thus, in his own self, in his own true nature, he became immortal.
The meaning is that, having previously attained all desires through self-knowledge by virtue of having achieved all that is desired even while living;
the repetition [of the word "having attained"] is for the purpose of demonstrating the completion of self-knowledge along with its fruit and its illustration. //6//
Thus ends the first section of the first chapter;
