the second chapter is completed.

[Now begins] the attainment of the fruit of the state of being the Self of all, which is brought about by the means of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), as illuminated by the Śruti through the lineage of teachers beginning with Vāmadeva and others.

Modern-day Brahmins who desire liberation, having encountered a highly renowned assembly of knowers of Brahman and desiring to know Brahman, wish to turn away from this transitory cycle of existence characterized by ends and means, which persists as long as life lasts; thus reflecting, they inquire of one another:
"Who is this Self? How so?
"Who is this whom we venerate as the Self?
Which one is that Self?"

That by which one sees, or that by which one hears, or that by which one smells odors, or that by which one articulates speech, or that by which one discerns what is sweet and what is not sweet. (AitU 3.1)
"We two worship that Self as 'This is the Self' directly; who is that Self?"—referring to that very Self which Vāmadeva, by worshipping directly as "This is the Self," became immortal.
"Who indeed is that Self?

Thus, as they questioned one another preceded by such a desire to know, there arose in them a memory produced by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the Śruti, which transcends the sphere of particular objects.

"He entered that Puruṣa by means of his two feet, saying, 'I am Brahman'; he split open this very suture and entered through that door—namely, this very Puruṣa. Here, two Brahmans are presented as being in mutual opposition;
and these two are the very self (ātman) of this body.
One or the other of those two must be the Self to be meditated upon. In order to determine which among them was to be meditated upon as the Self, they questioned one another again while deliberating.
As they were thus deliberating, their minds became focused on the specific subject matter for their investigation.
How so? Because in this single entity, two objects are perceived:
that by which one perceives through an instrument differentiated by many distinctions, and that which is perceived as a unity.

Because there is a reconnection of memory regarding objects perceived by other instruments of cognition, the self cannot, first of all, be that by which one perceives. But by what does one perceive? It is said: by that which, having become the eye, sees form.
Either by that which has become the ear, one hears sound; or by that which has become the nose, one smells odors;
or by that which has become the organ of speech, one articulates speech consisting of names, such as "cow," "horse," and so forth, as well as [the distinctions between] correct and incorrect.
Or rather, it is by that which has become the tongue that one discerns both the savory and the unsavory. //1//
But what is this single instrument that is said to be divided into many ways?
It is this: the heart and the mind;
perception, command, discernment, wisdom, intelligence, vision, fortitude, thought, deliberation, speed, and memory.
Volition, resolve, life-breath, desire, and control—all these are indeed names for consciousness.

As was stated previously: "The seed of creatures is the heart; the seed of the heart is the mind. Created by the mind are Water and Varuṇa; from the heart comes the mind, and from the mind comes the Moon.
Thus, this very heart and mind are one and the same, though they appear manifold.
By means of this single internal organ, when it becomes the eye, one sees form; when it becomes the ear, one hears; when it becomes the nose... [one smells].

It smells by becoming the nose; it speaks by becoming speech; it tastes by its own nature; it conceptualizes by means of the mind in the form of conceptualization; and it determines by means of the heart.
Therefore, this single instrument performs the functions of all the instruments and their objects for the sake of the perceiver’s apprehension of everything.
And likewise, among the Kauṣītakins: “Having mounted speech by means of wisdom (prajñā), one obtains all names through speech;
having mounted sight by means of wisdom, one obtains all forms through sight” (KauṣU 3.3), and so forth.
And in the Vājasaneyaka: “For with the mind alone one sees, with the mind one hears; for by means of the heart (hṛdaya) one knows forms” (BṛU 1.5.3), and so forth.
Therefore, it is well established that that which is denoted by the terms "heart" and "mind" is the cause of all perception.

And the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has that as its essence, for the Brāhmaṇa states: "That which is indeed *prāṇa* is wisdom (*prajñā*), and that which is indeed wisdom is *prāṇa*" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.3).
And we have already stated in the dialogue of the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*) and elsewhere that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) consists of a collection of instruments.

Therefore, that which entered through the feet is Brahman; however, because it serves as an instrument for the perceiver’s perception and is thus subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), that entity cannot be the Brahman that is the Self to be meditated upon.

By the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the functions of this heart—which is an instrument in the form of the mind (*manas*)—for the sake of the perceiver’s perception, are those that will be described hereafter.
They reached the certainty that "this perceived Self must be our [Self].

Those modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*)—which have as their object external and internal things and which exist for the purpose of perceiving Brahman, who is of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā-rūpa*) and resides within the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of that internal organ—are here called these:
*saṃjñānam* (perception), *saṃjñaptiḥ* (conception), and *cetanā-bhāvaḥ* (the state of consciousness).
Ājñāna is command, the state of being a lord; vijñāna is the thorough knowledge of the *kalās* and other categories;
prajñāna is wisdom, the state of being wise;
*medhā* is the capacity for retaining what has been learned; and *dṛṣṭi* is the perception of all objects through the doors of the senses.

Fortitude (*dhṛti*) is the sustaining of the body and senses when they have become dejected, by which their support is achieved—for it is said, "by fortitude one carries the body. Intellect (*mati*) is the act of thinking; wisdom (*manīṣā*) is independence therein. Speed (*jūti*) is the state of the mind being afflicted by pain and the like; memory (*smṛti*) is recollection.
*Saṃkalpa* is the conceptualizing of forms and so forth through modes such as white or black; *kratu* is determination; *asu* is the function that is the cause of life-activities such as breathing;
and *kāma* is thirst, the longing for objects not present at hand.

Control (*vaśaḥ*) is the desire for sexual union with women and so forth; such functions of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*), being for the sake of the perceiver—which is a mere designation and whose nature is pure consciousness—serve as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) for Brahman. Consequently, they become the qualities, names, and designations produced by those adjuncts, such as "conception" (*saṃjñāna*) and the rest.
All these are indeed names of intelligence (prajñāna), not by themselves directly;
and thus it has been said: "Only while breathing does it become what is called 'breath' (prāṇa)," and so forth (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7). //2//
This is Brahmā;
this is Indra;
this is Prajāpati.

All these are gods; and these five great elements— earth, wind, space, water, and light— as well as these other things, like various small seeds, those born from eggs, those born from wombs, those born from sweat, and those born from sprouts, such as horses and cattle.
Men, elephants, and whatever living beings there are— whether moving or flying, or whatever is stationary—
all that has wisdom as its eye;
it is established in wisdom.
The world has wisdom as its eye;
wisdom is its foundation;
Brahman is knowledge. (AitU 3.3)

This very Self, whose nature is consciousness, is Brahman—the supreme, the vital breath (prāṇa) residing within all bodies, the conscious self (prajñātman). Having entered into the limiting adjuncts of the internal organs, like the reflection of the sun in various portions of water, it is Hiraṇyagarbha, the vital breath, the conscious self. This same one is Indra by virtue of his qualities, the king of the gods; or rather, this is Prajāpati, the first-born embodied being.
He from whose mouth and other apertures the world-protectors such as Agni were born is this very Prajāpati;
all these gods, beginning with Agni, are he alone;
and these five great elements, earth and the rest, which constitute the material basis for all bodies and are characterized by the relationship of the eater and the eaten, are he alone.

Furthermore, these are "mixed with the minor" (*kṣudramiśrāṇi*), meaning they are as if mixed with minor or small things; the word "like" (*iva*) is redundant. Seeds such as those of snakes and so forth are the causes, and they are presented in two groups: which ones are they? They are said to be those born from eggs, such as birds and the like.
The womb-born are humans and the like;
the sweat-born are lice and the like;
and the soil-born are trees and the like.

Horses, cattle, men, elephants, and whatever other living beings there are—what are they? They are those that move, which travel on feet; and those that fly, which have the nature of soaring through the sky.
And whatever is stationary or immovable— all that is this very [Brahman];
all that, without exception, has wisdom as its eye.

Designation (*prajñapti*) is wisdom (*prajñā*), and that is indeed Brahman. That by which one is led is the "guide" (*netram*); that which has wisdom as its guide is "guided by wisdom" (*prajñānetram*).
This means it is established in wisdom—that is, in Brahman—at the times of its origination, persistence, and dissolution; it has wisdom as its support.
The world has wisdom as its eye, as before;
or rather, the entire world has the eye of wisdom, for wisdom is the foundation of the whole universe.
Therefore, Brahman is knowledge.

This very [reality], with all particular adjuncts extinguished, is stainless, pure, actionless, peaceful, one, and non-dual; it is to be known through the negation of all distinctions as "not this, not this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26), beyond the reach of all words and concepts.

Yet, through its connection with the adjunct of the inner-pure intellect (*prajñā*), it becomes the omniscient Lord (*īśvara*), the activator of the unmanifest seed of the universe common to all, and, by virtue of its governance, is designated as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*).
That very [Self] becomes known as Hiraṇyagarbha, characterized by the conceit of being the intellect (buddhi) which serves as the seed for the manifested world.
That same [Self], possessing the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the first body produced within the cosmic egg, becomes known as Virāṭ Prajāpati.
Possessing the limiting adjuncts of the elemental fire and so forth, it becomes known as the deities.
Likewise, even within the specific bodies that serve as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, Brahman acquires their respective names and forms.

That very same single reality, differentiated by the various distinctions of all limiting adjuncts, is known and conceptualized in manifold ways by all living beings and by philosophers in every possible manner:
"Some call this Agni, others Manu, and others Prajāpati."
"Some [worship] Indra, others Prāṇa, and others the eternal Brahman"—such is the Smṛti (Manu 12.123). //3//
Having ascended from this world by means of this wise Self, he attained all desires in that heavenly world and became immortal—yes, he became immortal. AitUp 3.4.

Whether he was Vāmadeva or someone else, whoever knows the Brahman as described above by means of that very self of wisdom—just as the ancient knowers became immortal through that same self of wisdom—this knower also, having departed from this world by means of that very self of wisdom, and so forth, has been explained.
Having departed from this world and attained all desires in that heavenly world, he became immortal; he became immortal. Om. //4//
Thus ends the first section of the third chapter.
The Upaniṣad is completed. Om tat sat.
